SOM.story:
In 2013 and 2014 the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), a force of soldiers sent by African countries to support the Somali government, had its headquarters and bases in Mogadishu. Human Rights Watch interviewed 50 people there, including 21 survivors. In a report published on 8 September 2014 it documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by AMISOM soldiers, mainly Ugandan soldiers at and around the headquarters and Burundian soldiers at their base.

Many of the women and girls had gone to the bases to ask for medicine or aid. Interpreters working for the force helped soldiers reach them, and some were pressed into sex in exchange for money, food or medicine. Four of the rapes and one sexual assault involved girls under 18. The youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013.

Children are also taken by the armed group Al-Shabaab, which is fighting the government. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia, 850 of them by Al-Shabaab, mainly to recruit them. In the same year it verified sexual violence against 267 children, 265 of them girls. Al-Shabaab was responsible for 120 of these cases and unidentified perpetrators for 110. Somali government security forces were responsible for 14, 11 of them by the Somali National Army, and Ethiopia's Liyu Police for 7. The UN Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

The UN's figures for 2024 show children in Somalia abused both by Al-Shabaab and by forces on the government's side, including its own army. The sources for this map record no prosecution of the AMISOM soldiers named in the 2014 report.

PAN.story:
In early February 2021 a subcommission of Panama's National Assembly, the country's parliament, reported that it had found abuse in shelters for children at social risk. The shelters were run privately or by charities and were supervised by the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf), the government agency for children and families. By March 2021 the Public Ministry, the national prosecution service, had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved elsewhere. Five people had been charged with offences including mistreatment of children, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman, an official who investigates complaints against public bodies, found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected and found that 70% of 44 shelters lacked suitable staff. The Ombudsman also said Senniaf did little to follow up on the shelters.

Panama also appears in cases that began in other countries. In Cartagena, Colombia, Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello, known as "La Madame", ran a network that supplied young women and girls under 18 to parties and sent women abroad to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas, coached to avoid checks at airports. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month in prison. On 23 October 2024 Panama's National Police and Public Ministry arrested a man in Puerto Caimito, in La Chorrera district, who was accused of contacting children through the gaming platform Roblox and threatening them to make them send sexual images. The alert came from Spanish police investigating a network that shared abuse material.

In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 5,275 web addresses hosted in Panama, 2% of its total.

The 2021 inspections found that the agency responsible for children's shelters did little to check on them, and the sources for this map do not record what changed afterwards. The online cases in Panama came to light through reports from foreign bodies, the British charity and the Spanish police.

LBR.story:
During Liberia's civil war, refugee children from Liberia, Guinea and Sierra Leone depended on aid agencies for food. In early 2002 a joint mission of UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, and the charity Save the Children UK reported that employees of charities, of UNHCR and of other UN bodies, as well as peacekeepers, were sexually exploiting refugee children in the three countries, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), the UN's internal investigators, then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10. In October 2002 OIOS said it had not substantiated any allegation against a UN staff member and had found no evidence of "widespread" abuse. Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think its report was wrong.

The war ended in 2003. In the years that followed, the number of private orphanages in Liberia rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia, the capital, was closed, and 89 of its 102 "orphans" were returned to their families. A 2007 report by UNICEF and Holt International, an adoption agency, found that many children had entered the adoption system through fraud, including false promises made to their birth parents, and the UN mission in Liberia found orphanages run for profit without accreditation. Between the US fiscal years 1994 and 2014 the United States issued 1,553 immigrant visas to children adopted from Monrovia, with the highest number, 353, in 2006. Canada placed a moratorium, a temporary ban, on adoptions from Liberia.

The sources for this map do not say how many of the children adopted abroad still had parents who had not agreed to give them up. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update, so the present scale of abuse in Liberia is not measured.

LBY.story:
Many migrants from Nigeria travel to Italy by way of Libya. In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN migration agency, said that perhaps 80 per cent of the Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy by sea could be victims of sex trafficking. Most of those it identified were between 13 and 24 years old, and its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. The Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM figures showing that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says commercial sex rings hold sub-Saharan women and girls in brothels in Libya, particularly in the southern towns of Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq, and that Nigerian women and girls are at greater risk. It cites an international organization's finding that 77 per cent of children and young people crossing Libya showed signs of exploitation amounting to trafficking. Observers quoted in the report describe officials taking part across the system, including the Libyan Coast Guard and immigration and security officials. The government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking.

Children crossing Libya pass through a country whose officials are reported to take part in trafficking and where no one has been prosecuted for it. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

ALB.story:
The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers exploit Albanian women and children for sex and forced labour, especially during the tourist season. Children from the Roma and Balkan-Egyptian minorities are forced to beg. Albanians who migrate to Western Europe, particularly to Britain, are at risk of being forced to commit crimes for others. In Britain in 2024, Albanians were the second most common nationality among people referred to the authorities as possible victims of trafficking, with 2,492 referrals, and 95 per cent of them were adults.

In the period the report covers, Albania's courts convicted two sex traffickers and two labour traffickers. These were the first trafficking convictions in the country since 2021.

Albanian courts convicted four traffickers after several years without a conviction, while Britain alone referred more than 2,000 Albanians as possible victims in a single year. Much of what is known about Albanian victims comes from the records of the countries they reach.

FJI.story:
In 1999 the Salesians of Don Bosco, a Catholic religious order present in more than 130 countries, moved the priest Julian Fox from Australia to Fiji after Australian police began investigating allegations that he had abused children. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. He was jailed in Australia in 2015.

In July 2020 the New Zealand broadcaster 1News reported about 1,300 alleged cases of child abuse by clergy in Fiji, and said some of them involved clergy from Australia and New Zealand. A survivor advocate told 1News that Fiji was a common destination for clergy transferred from those countries. Under the Vatican's rules, abuse cases against priests were reserved from 2001 to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the Vatican office for church discipline, under "pontifical secret", a rule of strict confidentiality that was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Australia and other countries found that bishops moved accused clergy and avoided going to the police.

No inquiry named in the sources for this map has examined the 1,300 alleged cases in Fiji, so it is not known how many involved priests sent from abroad.

TZA.story:
In the 1960s four priests of the Institute of Charity, a Catholic order known as the Rosminians, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's, a boarding school in Soni in Tanganyika, as Tanzania was then called. One of them was the English priest Kit Cunningham. The order acknowledged the crimes of the four priests, but in 2010 it refused to pay compensation. Cunningham died in December 2010. The abuse became public on 21 June 2011, when the BBC broadcast the documentary "Abused: Breaking the Silence". After the broadcast, 22 former Soni pupils pursued a compensation claim, and former pupils of Soni and of the order's Grace Dieu school in Leicestershire, England, announced they would sue. The case is recorded as settled.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking describes the present situation. It says children in Tanzania are exploited for sex, including by foreign visitors, and in forced labour and domestic servitude in Zanzibar, the islands off the coast, and that women and girls from the mainland are brought to Zanzibar with false promises. It also records child sex trafficking in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza, and says the government did not adequately deal with corruption and the involvement of officials.

The Soni abuse became known through a British broadcaster after Cunningham had died, and the former pupils pursued their claims against the order. The 2025 report describes child sex trafficking in Zanzibar and five mainland cities, and officials' involvement in it, that the government had not adequately addressed.

CMR.story:
In 2023 the UN verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon. It attributed 10 of the cases to the Cameroon Armed Forces, the national army, 6 to unidentified perpetrators and 1 to JAS, a faction of the armed group Boko Haram, which is active around Lake Chad. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 6 girls, one of them by the armed forces, and the abduction of 50 children. The UN publishes only the cases its staff have been able to confirm.

In 2023 most of the confirmed sexual violence against girls in Cameroon was committed by the country's own army. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update, so the full number of children affected is not known.

YEM.story:
In 2023 the UN verified sexual violence against 24 children in Yemen, 8 boys and 16 girls. It attributed 20 of the cases to the Yemen Armed Forces, the government's army, and to forces affiliated with them, including the police and the units called the Security Belt and the Amaliqah. The army itself was responsible for 9 cases and the police for 4. In 2024 the UN verified 11 cases, involving 6 boys and 5 girls. It attributed 2 to the Houthis, the armed movement fighting the government, 2 to the army and 7 to affiliated forces, 4 of them to the police. The UN publishes only the cases its staff have been able to confirm.

In both years most of the confirmed sexual violence against children in Yemen was committed by forces on the government's side, including the police. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

JOR.story:
Jordan hosts refugees from the war in Syria. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Syrian refugee women and girls in Jordan have been sold into forced marriages. In 2022 Jordanian authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.

The sources for this map record one investigation and do not say how many refugee girls in Jordan have been married by force. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

TWN.story:
Between 2003 and 2022 Taiwan sent 4,289 children abroad for intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child by parents in another country, according to figures compiled by the researcher Selman. Taiwan has not closed or suspended these adoptions.

In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, from two houses in Bangkok. They had been held there by Baby 101, a company that took orders for newborn babies from childless couples, and their passports had been taken from them. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking. Four of the women said they had been tricked, and Thailand's health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

Intercountry adoption from Taiwan continues, and the sources for this map record no investigation of how the children sent abroad came to be placed.

STP.story:
The research for this map found no documented case of child sexual abuse networks or child trafficking in São Tomé and Príncipe. The main source on online abuse of children is Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys, in which a sample of people are asked about their own experiences, into global estimates. In its 2026 update it had such surveys from only 60 countries, too few to represent West and Central Africa.

Without surveys or published cases, there is no measure of how many children in São Tomé and Príncipe are affected.

HUN.story:
In 2022 a Hungarian court sentenced Endre Kónya, the former deputy director of the children's home in Bicske, to three years and four months in prison for helping the home's director cover up his sexual abuse of children. In April 2023, before a visit by the Pope, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, and Kónya was among them. A presidential pardon in Hungary must be countersigned by a minister, and the justice minister at the time, Judit Varga, signed it. The pardon became public in early February 2024, when the news site Telex reported it on 2 February. People protested, and on 10 February Novák resigned, saying she had made a mistake. On the same day Varga announced that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Orbán then proposed a change to the constitution that would bar pardons for crimes against children.

Hungary also appears in several international police operations against online abuse. In 2018 Spanish police traced a private Skype group whose members in 14 countries exchanged abuse material, and by May 2018 eight people had been arrested in France, Hungary, Italy, Spain and Canada. An operation led by New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, begun in 2019 after an online service reported users exchanging images of the sadistic abuse of infants and children, had safeguarded 146 children by March 2022, and in Austria and Hungary some of the suspects were abusing their own children. In 2016 Europol, the EU's police agency, said criminals had built an organisation over 18 months to exploit migrants arriving in Europe, and that there had been many arrests in Germany and Hungary.

Between 2003 and 2022 Hungary sent 2,868 children abroad for intercountry adoption, according to figures compiled by the researcher Selman, and it has not closed these adoptions.

The pardon of a man convicted of covering up abuse in a state children's home led the president and the former justice minister to leave office. The sources for this map do not say whether the proposed ban on such pardons was passed.

BOL.story:
In 1964 the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas first abused a child in Lima, Peru, and afterwards he settled in Bolivia. The Jesuits, the Catholic religious order called the Society of Jesus, made him deputy director of the Juan XXIII boarding school in Cochabamba in October 1971, and about three years later he became its director. In 1978, in Spain, he told his Jesuit instructor about the abuse. No church process was opened and he was not removed from his work with children. He died in Cochabamba in September 2009 and was never prosecuted. On 30 April 2023 the Spanish newspaper El País published his diary, in which he admits abusing dozens of children at schools in Latin America, mainly in Cochabamba, and estimates the number at about 85. El País reported that at least seven provincial superiors, the heads of the order's regional branches, and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics had covered up his crimes.

Bolivia also has closed farming colonies of conservative Mennonites, a German-speaking Protestant community, with about 150,000 members by an estimate for 2023. In the Manitoba Colony, men sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate whole households, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. At first the attacks were blamed on ghosts or demons. They came to light in June 2009, and in August 2011 a Bolivian court convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls. Seven were sentenced to 25 years and an eighth man to 12 years for supplying the drug. A 2013 investigation reported similar attacks continuing.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says foreign offenders exploit children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, around Rurrenabaque, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It says the production of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, and that Bolivian women and girls are exploited for sex in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru.

The Jesuit case was known to the order from 1978 and was published only after Pedrajas had died, so no court ever heard it. The 2025 report shows children in Bolivia now exploited by foreign visitors and through abuse material sold online.

SDN.story:
In April 2023 war broke out between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force. The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan, a body of investigators appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, found that rape and gang rape were widespread, committed mostly by men in RSF uniform and by militias allied with them, and that the victims included girls as young as 8. It found that the RSF's abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes amounted to sexual slavery. Some cases were committed by the Sudanese Armed Forces. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023, 57 of them by the RSF, and against 74 children in 2024, 54 by the RSF and 9 by militias affiliated with it. He listed the RSF among the forces responsible for the rape and abduction of children.

Girls from neighbouring countries are also brought into Sudan. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes controlled with drugs. In 2022 the UN attributed 4 of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to the Chadian National Army.

In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France, saying they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region. The authorities found that most of the children were from Chad and were not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children, and a Sudanese defendant was sentenced to four years.

In the war that began in 2023, the UN found that most of the sexual violence against children in Sudan was committed by the RSF. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in the Middle East and North Africa in its 2026 update to measure abuse there.

MLI.story:
In 2012 and 2013 the armed groups Ansar Eddine and AQIM, an affiliate of al-Qaeda, ran an Islamic police force in Timbuktu. The International Criminal Court (ICC), the permanent international court for war crimes, later tried Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz for his role in that period. On 26 June 2024 it convicted him of crimes against humanity and war crimes, including torture and persecution, but acquitted him of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery, charges that included the forced marriage of women and girls.

The fighting continued in the following years. In 2023 the UN verified the rape of 15 girls in Mali, 4 of them by the Malian armed forces. In 2024 it verified the rape of 32 girls: 22 by unidentified perpetrators, 4 by ISGS, the Islamic State group in the Sahel, 3 by JNIM, an al-Qaeda-linked coalition, 2 by the Malian armed forces and 1 by the militia Ganda Lassal Izo. It also verified the abduction of 119 children that year, 4 of them by foreign security personnel.

Children from Mali are also moved across West Africa. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says Nigerian networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire, and that in Senegal's Kédougou gold-mining region girls as young as 12 are exploited for sex, some of them from Mali. In September 2019 police in Kaduna, Nigeria, raided a building signed as an Islamic studies centre and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them chained; some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana, and seven people claiming to be teachers were arrested.

The UN's yearly counts show the Malian army among those responsible for raping girls, and the ICC case ended without a conviction for sexual violence. Childlight, a research centre that combines representative surveys into global estimates of online abuse, found too few such surveys in West and Central Africa in its 2026 update, so the wider scale of abuse is not known.

IDN.story:
Between 1967 and 1997 or 1998 Dutch couples adopted children from Indonesia and other countries through licensed Dutch agencies. In 2019 the Netherlands set up the Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, chaired by Tjibbe Joustra. In February 2021 it reported "serious violations" in adoptions from countries including Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia, and concluded that the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent the abuses. The government said its officials had known of wrongdoing for years and had not intervened, and on 8 February 2021 it suspended all intercountry adoptions.

Babies are still being sold abroad from Indonesia. In July 2025 police in West Java said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some of them "reserved while still in the womb", for 11 to 16 million rupiah each. The syndicate prepared false family cards and passports in Pontianak. Police arrested 13 people, rescued six babies who were about to be sold, and asked Interpol, the international police organisation, to help trace the adoptive parents.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says the sexual exploitation of children by foreign visitors is common in the Riau Islands, which border Singapore, and that women and girls are forced into commercial sex, notably in Batam. It also says tourists from the Middle East pay more than $700 for week-long "contract marriages" in Puncak, in Bogor, involving girls as young as nine, and that the government tacitly accepted the practice. The report says corruption and the complicity of officials seriously held back efforts against trafficking.

In the recent cases the buyers came mainly from Singapore and the Middle East, and the government is reported to have tolerated the contract marriages. The Dutch inquiry covered only adoptions into the Netherlands, and the sources for this map record no inquiry into adoptions from Indonesia to other countries.
